Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Chicago/Romeoville, IL
702 PM CDT Sun Aug 9 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Renewed thunderstorm development is expected over portions of
  the area late this evening and overnight, some of which could
  be strong to severe.

- Training of heavy thunderstorms (2"/hr+ rainfall rates) over 
  the same areas late this evening and overnight may lead to 
  flash flooding.

- Additional periods of storms are expected Monday through mid-
  week. Some of these storms could be severe, especially late
  Monday afternoon or Monday night and lead to additional
  flooding.

&&

.UPDATE...
Issued at 700 PM CDT Sun Aug 9 2026

- Flash Flood Watch issued for much of northeast IL and
  northwest IN late this evening through early Monday AM.

Concerns are increasing that a corridor of training 
thunderstorms (capable of rainfall rates in excess of 2 inches 
per hour) will set up somewhere over northeast Illinois into 
northwest Indiana.

The combination of several factors have led us to issue a Flash
Flood Watch for portions of northeast Illinois and northwest
Indiana. High PWATs upwards of 2", the nose of a strengthening
low-level jet oriented into the area atop a stalled surface 
boundary, and saturated areas from the first round of storms
over portions of the Chicago metro. This is in effect from 9 PM
CDT through 7 AM CDT Monday.

Those that live in especially flood prone areas should monitor
trends closely through this evening and methods to receive
warning information that will wake you up.

Not to be overshadowed, the severe threat will continue
overnight, with the primary threat being damaging wind gusts.
Large hail will be possible with the strongest storms. We will
also be monitoring a non-zero tornado threat with any storms
that develop along and south of the stalled surface front.

Petr

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 132 PM CDT Sun Aug 9 2026

We have been able to destabilize ahead of the morning line of
convection as a northward moving warm front has made steady
northward progress. 3000 J/Kg of MLCAPE is mostly uncapped at
this point, and there is a narrow ribbon of enhanced DCAPE 
nosing into the Chicago area. The stronger lead shortwave is 
largely moving through here over the next few hours, and this
will keep a marginal severe thunderstorm risk in place through
mid afternoon. The main concern would be these transient
downburst signatures in the more mature developed line of
storms along with a few instances of hail. The orientation these
storms are taking will also lead to varying water levels near
the shore in wake of these storms, so the sea will remain
hazardous even after the storms pass this afternoon. 

As far as the rest of the day is concerned farther south, the 
battle will be between the arriving mid level shortwave sliding 
through the area versus some capping reinforcement from lower 
level warm advection and anvil shielding from ongoing 
convection. Colder temperatures aloft are focused north of
I-80. Therefore, with an uncapped environment, expect some
isolated to widely scattered storms farther south given that
forcing is more muted. The signal then continues for a bit of a
lull in activity as shortwave forcing temporarily eases, and 
capping will get reinforced via an uptick in warm air advection

After that we will have to take a look and see where the surface 
warm front will set up this evening. The pattern tonight has 
some similarity to a Maddox flash flood setup, with a low 
amplitude shortwave, upper jet to the north, and a substantial 
low level jet progged. How much of mesohigh influence is a bit 
more vague in the latest guidance. PMM/LPMM guidance (from 0z/ 
6z) had some hefty rain totals ( 4-7" in the region). The signal
is a little more muted in latest guidance, at least on the 
footprint of the heavy rainfall, but the flash flood potential 
this evening is still elevated. The warm front has moved into 
the Chicago metro area, and it seems like that is where it will 
remain into the evening hours. Forecast soundings do still 
suggest, in spite of some disagreements in low level jet 
strength and orientation with respect to the warm front, a 
period this evening into the early overnight where slow storm 
motions would be favored very strong lift (lower level moisture 
convergence), even if not quite as long lived as considered 
before. The most concerning time frame still looks to be in the 
mid evening through early overnight across the Chicago area 
before the low level jet veers more to westerly. As this occurs 
the area of concern would shift to east Central IL (Kankakee 
area) and into NW Indiana. There is still considerable 
uncertainty here on coverage, but the signs are there to 
continue this message tonight. 

The forcing during the day on Monday is not as clear and 
confidence on storm evolution on Monday is somewhat low. The 
warm front will briefly shift south (or to southern portions of 
our area) during the morning hours, however the low level flow 
will turn back around to the southwest. Any weak ripples in the 
flow aloft though could a trigger a storm or two during the 
afternoon. Deeper forcing may not arrive until the evening with
a very warm. moist and unstable air mass in place coupled with
strong deep layer shear. This environment would support all
hazards initially and also eventually bowing/line structures.  
Another flash flood threat would be in place, especially with
another uptick in the low level jet Monday evening. We will have
to watch where the warm/stationary front lays out tomorrow, with
high uncertainty on that. 

Unfortunately the pattern looks fairly active with a warm/moist 
airmass in place and a endless stream of shortwaves moving through 
in northwest flow upon a lingering frontal boundary Tuesday and 
Wednesday.  A more dynamic system will move through eastern Canada 
later in the week, and this will help to move the frontal boundary 
farther south. This will take the storm track with it, and also lead 
to cooler onshore flow in this system's wake Thursday and Friday. 

KMD

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TAFS THROUGH 06Z TUESDAY/...
Issued at 700 PM CDT Sun Aug 9 2026

Key aviation forecast messages:

- Waves of TSRA likely late this evening through tonight with 
  gusty winds and rainfall rates >2"/hr

- Low confidence in SHRA/TSRA trends on Monday

A narrow axis of showers with isolated embedded TS has pushed
out over Lake Michigan with a lull in precipitation expected 
for the next 2-3 hours before additional SHRA/TSRA development 
occurs. It remains uncertain exactly where this corridor will 
set up but the location of a stalled surface boundary near the
I-80 corridor suggests that this may occur very near or 
directly over the terminals. 

Have maintained TEMPOs for TS from 3-7Z to account for this
potential and extended the duration of the VCTS mention through
10Z for the Chicago metro terminals. Once trends become more
clear prevailing TS will likely be needed for portions of the 
overnight hours. Gusty winds will likely accompany the strongest
storms in addition to torrential rainfall (rates >2"/hr 
possible).

Looking ahead to the day on Monday, confidence in SHRA/TSRA
trends remain very low and will likely be dependent up on how
things unfold overnight and whether the surface boundary shifts
farther south or remains in place near the terminals. For now 
have left the TAFs dry. There could be several hours of SHRA/TS 
during this period but identifying when and where this were to 
occur remains too low confidence to include with this update.

Winds will be southeast to southerly this evening (outside of 
any gusty thunderstorm winds) becoming light and variable 
overnight. Winds then trend toward a prevailing light east to 
northeast during the day on Monday.

Petr

.AVIATION /06Z TAFS THROUGH 12Z TUESDAY/...
Issued at 131 AM CDT Mon Aug 10 2026

Key Messages:

- Scattered showers and possibly a few storms will continue 
  near the terminals overnight.

- There is a potential for MVFR (or lower) ceilings and/or
  visibilities through this morning.

- Additional waves of showers and storms are possible at and
  near the terminals today, but a high degree of uncertainty 
  remains regarding the timing and coverage of this activity.


The worst of tonight's thunderstorm activity has pushed east and
south of the terminals, but scattered showers will continue to
fester near the terminals for at least a few more hours tonight.
A few additional storms may develop, but their coverage should
be more isolated and they should be less intense than the
earlier storms.

Patchy MVFR ceilings have developed in the wake of the earlier
thunderstorm activity, and the expectation is for the footprint
of these lower ceilings to expand later overnight and past
daybreak. Some sites could hold onto MVFR ceilings well into
this afternoon, but confidence in ceiling trends is low on the
whole. Additionally, fog may also develop overnight as a result
of the excess low-level moisture in the area. The greatest 
signal for visibility reductions across the latest available 
forecast guidance suggests that RFD is the most likely of our 
TAF sites to be affected by this, but observational trends will 
need to be monitored closely.

Additional showers and thunderstorms may develop in the area
later today, but the exact timing and coverage of this potential
activity remains highly uncertain. Opted to introduce two PROB30
groups into the TAFs to highlight the time windows when
convection is most likely to affect the terminals. The first
window is tied to a convectively-enhanced disturbance that may
emanate from the central Plains tonight and reach our area
towards midday/the early afternoon. It is not yet clear how
well-defined this disturbance will be, whether we'll still be 
capped for stronger surface-based thunderstorms to develop 
as it arrives, and whether the axis that the potential 
thunderstorm may focus along will remain south of the terminals,
so opted to carry -SHRA in this PROB30 group for now as just 
seeing some scattered high-based showers is also very much a 
possibility during this time window. The second window is tied 
to another upper-level disturbance that is progged to arrive 
sometime late this afternoon or evening. Thunderstorms, 
including strong to severe thunderstorms with strong winds and 
hail, appear to be more likely to occur during this time window
compared to earlier, but exactly where and when they will 
develop remains uncertain. All in all, a lot of uncertainty 
remains regarding the thunderstorm potential for later today, 
and additional changes to the TAFs will likely be needed as 
observational trends become clearer.

Lastly, confidence in wind direction trends for today is also 
fairly low, largely as a result of the thunderstorm-related 
uncertainties. Outside of any thunderstorm influence though, 
surface flow should remain at or under 10 kts through the TAF 
period with a generally easterly or northeasterly direction 
favored at ORD, MDW, and GYY from around midday through tonight 
as a result of a weak lake breeze/onshore flow.

Ogorek

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 300 AM CDT Mon Aug 10 2026

Forecast remains complex through mid-week, as a nearly 
stationary frontal boundary lingers across the forecast area 
beneath an active west-northwest flow pattern aloft. Periodic 
shower and thunderstorm chances will persist with somewhat low 
confidence in timing and coverage, ultimately modulated by 
individual short waves and daily diurnal heating and instability
trends. Episodes of severe weather and locally heavy rainfall 
remain possible.

In the near-term, latest surface analysis depicts a nearly 
stationary frontal boundary stretching from an area of low 
pressure over western KS northeast into western IA, then east 
along roughly the I-80 corridor across northern IL/northwest IN.
A very warm/humid airmass is in place along/south of the 
boundary, characterized by temps in the upper 70/around 80 and 
dew points in the mid-70s at this late night hour. Aloft, 
seasonably fast west-northwest flow was in place across the 
region, supplying a track for a series of mid-level short wave 
disturbances of varying amplitude. One such wave is currently 
tracking from IA into northern IL, supporting a southwesterly 35
kt low-level jet atop the low-level frontal zone into northeast
IL/northwest IN. Several clusters of strong thunderstorms had 
developed in the enhanced warm/moist advection regime associated
with this jet last evening, with a small MCS remaining across 
our southern tier of cwa counties as of 2 AM on the nose of the 
jet in the vicinity of the surface frontal boundary. Given 
ML/MUCAPE values in the 3000-3500 J/kg range, 35-40 kts of 
effective shear and precipitable water values near 2 inches, 
severe weather and locally heavy rainfall remain a concern with
these storms for the next hour or so, before they eventually 
slide southeast of the area toward/just after daybreak as the 
low-level jet gradually veers more westerly and weakens with the
passage of the mid-level wave.

Once these storms exit the area, there should be a bit of a 
lull in convection in the wake of the departing short wave and 
during our diurnal instability minimum. Can't completely rule 
out some isolated elevated shower or thunderstorm development 
however, due to the presence of the front/baroclinic boundary 
and weaker but still persistent warm/moist advection. Chances 
should increase again at least a bit toward midday and into this
afternoon however, as another weak wave or MCV (currently 
approaching the Omaha vicinity) tracks east during a more 
favorable diurnal time. CAM guidance loosely depicts this, 
though differences in coverage and timing details are evident. 
Additional development also appears possible later this evening,
as the nocturnal low-level jet modestly increases atop the 
frontal zone. There does appear to be a somewhat consistent 
signal however, amongst both CAM and global guidance, for an MCS
to develop over NE/SD later tonight which would approach the 
forecast area around/after daybreak Tuesday. This supports the 
highest pops (60-70%) during Tuesday, and have limited other 
mentions to just chance (20-40%) later today and tonight. Given 
otherwise similar instability/shear and moisture parameters, we 
remain in SPC/WPC slight risks for severe weather and excessive 
rainfall during these periods. 

No significant change in the pattern is evident into mid-week 
(Wednesday, possibly Thursday), though confidence gradually 
decreases based on impacts of any preceding convective/MCS 
outflow impacts. Global ensembles continue to show a signal for 
our frontal boundary to shift a little farther south Thursday 
night and Friday, which may decrease our shower/thunderstorm 
potential briefly late in the week, though this signal is weaker
than earlier runs and there are indications that the front may 
lift back into the area next weekend. Thus, it appears that our 
seasonably warm/humid and periodically stormy pattern may 
persist for much of the forecast period.

Ratzer

mesoanalysis would support storm organization and an associated 
severe (primarily wind/hail) threat as evidenced by the 
scattered supercell storms currently over LM/IWX's cwa.

far southeast South Dakota, which may evolve into a more 
widespread and potentially significant severe weather threat 
across our forecast area later this morning and early afternoon.

eventually growing upscale into a forward-propagating MCS across
northwest IA/southwest MN over the next few hours and 
eventually tracking east-southeast along the corridor strong 
instability along the aforementioned frontal zone into northern 
IL toward mid-late morning. The combination of unseasonably 
strong westerly mid-level flow and resulting deep shear(50+ kts 
at 700 mb), steep mid-level lapse rates (near 8 C/km) MUCAPE 
values in excess of 3500 J/kg, the potential for significant 
severe weather appears rather high. Several CAMs are depicting 
pockets surface wind gusts of 80+ mph with this MCS across 
portions of the forecast area. A tornado threat would also 
likely exist given sufficient low-level shear and the proximity 
of the previously mentioned surface frontal boundary. While the 
exact evolution of this MCS remains uncertain, SPC's Day 1 
enhanced (level 3 of 5) for out forecast area appears warranted.
Currently timing of this threat looks to be from perhaps 9 AM 
in our northwest cwa through around 3 PM in the far east. There 
may also be some convective development along the front ahead of
the MCS, if a strong MCV develops prior to reaching the cwa 
increases warm-advection ascent ahead of the main cluster as 
indicated by some of the CAMs.

wasn't enough, we'll also need to monitor the location of heavy 
rainfall and flooding potential - particularly for the urbanized
Chicago metro area as well as locations which saw 3-5"+ of 
rainfall Sunday and evening. Had contemplated issuing a flood 
watch, though with current predawn convection slow to fill-in 
(so far) and some uncertainty remaining with the evolution of 
the MCS later this morning, elected to hold off at this time 
pending some further clarity on location of higher rainfall 
impacts.

remnant cold pool and how far south the effective frontal zone

uncertainty is how far south an area of surface high pressure 
builds across the western Lakes in the Friday/Saturday period.

for the local area.

support a stronger storm or two. Since most of these storms
should be elevated and the lapse rates upstairs are somewhat

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 130 PM CDT Fri Aug 14 2026

...THREAT FOR SIGNIFICANT FLASH FLOODING TONIGHT...

Early afternoon surface charts depict an elongated stationary 
front extending from central Virginia along the Ohio River 
northwestward toward Kansas City, Missouri. A series of mid- 
level perturbations are riding along and north as the front as 
evident by festering areas of showers and thunderstorms from 
Omaha, Nebraska to Indianapolis, Indiana. The western-most 
perturbation (near Omaha) is the strongest in the region, as 
demonstrated by broad anticyclonic upper-level venting depicted in
mid-level water vapor imagery as well as a clear cyclonic low- 
level circulation (a "warm-core" low) being sampled by both 
KOAX/KDMX WSR-88D radars. 

This evening, the Omaha warm-core low pressure system will 
shift eastward and encounter an increasingly unstable airmass 
(MUCAPE > 3000 J/kg) across southern Iowa. Rapid thunderstorm 
development and associated regions of latent heat release will 
be poised to intensify the warm core low west of the Mississippi
River by midnight, leading to augmented low-level moisture 
transport north of the stalled front and into the circulation. 
Intense moisture convergence will lead to unusually high 
tropical-like moisture values with mean PWATs forecasted to 
approach 2.5" (near all-time records per sounding climatology at
ILX/DVN) ahead of the low. Taken altogether, a cluster of 
thunderstorms with intense rain rates (3 to 5"/hr) is expected 
to develop and move into northern Illinois during the pre-dawn 
hours of Saturday morning. (This process is not unlike how 
tropical systems intensify and produce intense rain rates). 

While the center of the warm core low is expected to track more
or less along the I-88 or I-80 corridors during the morning 
hours, the west-to-east orientation axis of the instability axis
south of the core should promote the highest coverage of 
thunderstorms near and south of I-80. The thunderstorms are 
expected to reach the I-39 corridor sometime in the 1 to 3 AM 
timeframe, and then the I-55 and I-57 corridors sometime in the 
2 to 5 AM timeframe, and then northwestern Indiana after 5 AM. 
The back edge of thunderstorms would then work eastward through 
the area after daybreak, perhaps not clearing northwestern 
Indiana until the 10 AM to 1 PM timeframe. 

Owing to the repeated rounds of thunderstorms this past week, 
soils along and south of I-88 are saturated and prone to cause 
widespread flooding with as little as one half to one inch of 
rain. Even with the expectation for the warm-core low and 
associated region of heavy rain to be somewhat progressive 
tonight (moving quickly rather than staying over the same exact 
area), the intensity of rain rates should still nevertheless 
lead to a swath of 3 to 6 inches of rain (locally higher), as 
supported by 12Z HREF and REFS 24-hour LPMM QPF. Such rainfall 
over saturated soils would lead to widespread significant flash 
flooding including widespread road closures and even structure 
flooding. Accordingly, a rare Level 3 out of 4 flash flood 
threat has been issued by WPC for areas along and south of I- 80
(primarily along and south of a line from Mendota, Illinois to 
Fowler, Indiana). 

A Flood Watch for flash flooding has been issued across much of
northern Illinois in two segments. The first segment is along 
and south of I-80 and features heightened wording for 
significant flash flooding. The second segment is along the I-88
corridor for somewhat lower confidence flash flooding should 
the track of the warm core low and associated region of 
thunderstorms track further north than currently expected. Both 
segments will be in effect from 10 PM this evening through 10 AM
tomorrow. 

Not to be forgotten, cannot rule out locally damaging winds 
along the leading edge of the thunderstorm cluster tonight. Even
if winds do not technically meet severe criteria (58 mph), the 
saturated soils may allow for trees to fall easier than in 
typical conditions. At this point, currently see the threat for 
severe weather as secondary to the threat of flash flooding. 


Saturday Afternoon onward:

In the wake of the warm-core low, a few showers and areas of 
drizzle may linger as late as the afternoon. However, current 
thinking is that coverage should markedly decrease during the 
late morning and early afternoon hours. Attention then turns 
toward the next upper-level wave and an associated cold front 
due to sweep across the area late Saturday night into Sunday. Am
noting a trend toward less instability ahead of the front which
may limit the coverage of showers and storms across our area,
but it remains to be seen if such a trend will continue. So, will
maintain mid-range chance PoPs (30% or so) across the area 
through Sunday morning.

A surface high pressure system will move into the Great Lakes 
in the wake of the front and facilitate a much-needed break from
this incredibly stormy pattern. Monday and at least the first 
half of Tuesday look completely dry before a series of storm 
systems move through the general region by midweek.

shift eastward and encounter an increasingly unstable airmass 
(MUCAPE > 3000 J/kg) across southern Iowa. Rapid thunderstorm 
development and associated regions of latent heat release will 
be poised to intensify the warm core low west of the Mississippi

transport north of the stalled front and into the circulation.

tropical-like moisture values with mean PWATs forecasted to 
approach 2.5" (near all-time records per sounding climatology at

thunderstorms with intense rain rates (3 to 5"/hr) is expected 
to develop and move into northern Illinois during the pre-dawn 
hours of Saturday morning. (This process is not unlike how 
tropical systems intensify and produce intense rain rates).

or less along the I-88 or I-80 corridors during the morning 
hours, the west-to-east orientation axis of the instability axis
south of the core should promote the highest coverage of 
thunderstorms near and south of I-80. The thunderstorms are 
expected to reach the I-39 corridor sometime in the 1 to 3 AM 
timeframe, and then the I-55 and I-57 corridors sometime in the

the area after daybreak, perhaps not clearing northwestern 
Indiana until the 10 AM to 1 PM timeframe.

widespread flooding with as little as one half to one inch of

thunderstorms track further north than currently expected. Both 
segments will be in effect from 10 PM this evening through 10 AM

severe weather as secondary to the threat of flash flooding.

drizzle may linger as late as the afternoon. However, current

late morning and early afternoon hours. Attention then turns 
toward the next upper-level wave and an associated cold front 
due to sweep across the area late Saturday night into Sunday. Am

this incredibly stormy pattern. Monday and at least the first 
half of Tuesday look completely dry before a series of storm 
systems move through the general region by midweek.

forward to.

A shortwave trough continues to pivot across northern IL and 
has lead to the development of a cluster of thunderstorms. This 
cluster of thunderstorms will continue to push east across 
northwest IN through the early overnight hours before exiting 
our area. The main threat with this storm cluster will be 
torrential downpours, but some localized pockets of gusty winds 
(upwards of 45-50 mph) have been occurring and that will likely 
continue as the cluster moves across our northwest IN counties. 
Given that this cluster is moving rather quickly, the flooding 
threat with it appears to be low. 

In the wake of this cluster, light to moderate stratiform 
showers will persist through the predawn hours. However, 
additional showers and thunderstorms are developing in northern 
MO and west-central IL along the remnant outflow boundary from 
last night's storms. Latest radar trends show that these 
developing showers/storms may stay just south of our forecast 
area, however, if any development can occur further north then 
portions of Livingston, Ford, and Iroquois Counties would be in 
play. Given that the steering flow and forcing are oriented 
parallel to the outflow, showers/storms in central and north-
central IL will likely train over the same areas. Couple this 
with the 2.0 inch PWATs and the modest instability and 
conditions are primed for another period of torrential rainfall.
If the heaviest rainfall does occur over our southern areas, 
then a threat for significant flash flooding would quickly 
materialize as these areas have already seen nearly 6-10 inches 
of rain over the past few days. Due to this threat a Flash Flood
Watch was issued earlier this evening and remains in effect 
until 10 AM CDT this morning for areas near and south of I-80 
where the flooding threat is greatest. 

The showers and storms tonight are expected to gradually wane 
around daybreak as the low-level jet weakens and the 
aforementioned shortwave pushes east of the area. However, a 
cold front (which is currently analyzed along a Sioux City, IA 
to Minneapolis, MN line) will be moving across northern IL and 
northwest IN today. Initially, it looks as if the atmosphere 
should be stable enough to keep dry conditions around through 
much of the morning, but another shortwave is expected to pivot 
across southern IA and north-central IL this afternoon. As this 
wave approaches the front is forecast to be near the I-55 
corridor which is where the focus for additional showers and 
storms this afternoon should reside. That said, forecast 
soundings do continue to show some weak capping in place and 
with the bulk of the wave's forcing forecast to be aimed into 
central IL it seems shower and storm coverage locally will be 
more hit and miss. For now have opted to maintain some 20-30% 
chances for showers and thunderstorms in the forecast, mainly 
for areas southeast of I- 55, but suspect many locations should 
remain dry especially those to the north of I-55. Regardless, 
the threat for severe weather with any storms today is low due 
to the lack of wind shear though heavy downpours and locally 
gusty winds will still be possible.

allowing a surface high to start building in from the north.

pattern for Monday and most of the day on Tuesday. Therefore, 
expect mostly to partly sunny skies both days with highs in the 
low to mid-80s and overnight lows in the 60s. Unfortunately, the
nice weather won't last long as another shortwave and its 
associated cold front are forecast to dive through the Midwest 
Tuesday night into the day on Wednesday. This system will bring 
more chances for showers and thunderstorms to the region as 
early as Tuesday evening, but the bulk of the stormy weather 
should occur overnight Tuesday night into Wednesday. While 
confidence is high on showers/storms occurring during this 
period, there continues to be some uncertainty in exact timing 
and intensity so make sure to stay updated as we get closer. 

On the bright side, long range ensemble guidance continues to 
hint that high pressure should move in behind Wednesday's storm 
system which looks to keep the bulk of any additional storms 
south and west of us for the later half of the week. Though if 
this does occur it looks as if temperatures may be more on the 
seasonably cool side with highs in the 70s and lows in the 50s 
to 60s.

in the gridded forecast to account for this near Lake Michigan 
and as far west as I-355. However, most areas are expected to 
remain dry today even if these showers develop.

the aforementioned convergence axis sets up, with upper 70s to 
lower 80s farther inland and low to mid 70s closer to the lake.
Diurnal mixing to the west of this axis should also help keep 
heat indices in check compared to yesterday. Temperatures 
tonight are forecast to drop into the low to mid 60s for most of
the area. If high clouds are slower to drift into the area 
overnight, temperatures may manage to drop into the upper 50s 
across portions of interior northern Illinois.

waves/vorts are forecast to move within the broader northwest 
flow aloft across the area in the afternoon and night. This may
lead to the development of thunderstorms across southern
Wisconsin and northern Illinois in the afternoon that moves 
southeast across the rest of the area into the evening and 
overnight hours. While there may be some capping initially to 
limit coverage, any storms that develop will have the potential 
to become severe, especially near and north of I-80 where deep 
layer shear will be the highest (upwards of 40 to 50 kts). The
flooding threat may be more localized initially with a more
discrete mode, however, if storms transition toward multicell 
clusters or redevelop over the same areas into the evening and 
overnight hours, flash flooding would become a greater concern.

guidance with respect to shower/storm coverage here locally, 
likely owing to differences in the strength of the capping and 
position and strength of the low-level jet. Given some of these 
uncertainties, SPC and WPC have maintained a level 1 of 5 
threat for severe weather and level 1 of 4 threat for flash 
flooding respectively. However, am becoming a bit more concerned
that a conditionally higher severe and flash flooding threat 
may unfold over at least portions of the area and will continue 
to message this potential. Will have to monitor trends closely 
over the next 24 hours.

Thursday as a cooler and less humid airmass settles into the 
area in the wake of a cold front late Tuesday night/early 
Wednesday AM. Temperatures will be cooler (typically lower 80s 
for mid August) with highs in the mid to upper 70s each day 
amidst cooler onshore flow. Confidence in the details then 
decreases late week into the upcoming weekend as additional 
waves move within the upper level northwest flow pattern, with a
potentially more robust and slower moving wave bringing 
increasing shower/storm chances for the weekend.
